title: How to get more views on TikTok on a small account
author: Julia Tovmasyan
content_snippet: Work out which part of your video lost the audience, fix that, and turn the views into earnings through paid briefs rather than waiting on a follower count.
content_full:
A video with no views is not being punished, it is being tested and failing the test. TikTok shows almost everything to a small group first and decides what happens next from how that group behaves. Getting more views means giving that first group a reason to stay, and knowing which part of your video lost them. Once views arrive, they are also worth money, and not only through the route most people assume.

Why your video is not getting views

Start from what the system is actually reading.

TikTok has said follower count is not a direct factor in what its recommendation system shows, and that recommendations are built from three kinds of signal: how people interact with a video, information about the video itself such as captions, sounds and hashtags, and account settings like language and country.

That has a practical consequence. Nothing about your account is holding the video back. The video is being judged on its own, which is the good news and the uncomfortable news at once.

Diagnose before you change anything

Most advice tells you to post more. Work out what went wrong first, because the fix differs depending on where people left.

They left in the first second. The opening did not give a reason to stay. Nothing else in the video matters yet.

They left around a third of the way in. The opening promised something the video then delayed. This is the most common one, and the fix is usually cutting the setup rather than improving it.

They watched it through and nothing happened. No shares, no comments, no repeat views. The video was fine and forgettable, which is a harder problem than a bad opening.

It did well once and never again. That was a one-off subject rather than a repeatable format, and the account has nothing to build on.

Check your own retention graph before rewriting anything. The moment people leave is rarely where you assume.

What TikTok is actually reading

TikTok names three kinds of signal behind its recommendations, and each one points at a different thing you control.

How people interact with the video. Whether they finish it, replay it, send it, or comment. Rewatches matter more here than on most feeds, because a short loop can be watched three times by the same person, and each pass counts. This is why quick reveals and tight loops travel further than their runtime suggests.

Information about the video itself. Captions, sounds, and hashtags are named explicitly. They are not decoration added after the edit, they are part of what the system reads to work out who might want this. A generic sound and three broad hashtags tell it very little.

Account and device settings. Language and country, which you do not control, but which explain why a video can do well in one market and vanish in another.

Nothing in that list is your follower count. TikTok has said outright it is not a direct factor, which is the whole reason a small account can put a video in front of a large audience.

Things that do not fix it

Four common responses, none of which addresses the problem.

Posting more often. More copies of a video with the same weakness produce more videos with that weakness. Frequency multiplies whatever you already have, including the flaw.

Deleting and reposting. The video does not get a fresh start, and you lose whatever data the first attempt gave you about where people left.

Adding hashtags. More tags do not widen reach on their own. Specific ones that describe the actual subject do more than a pile of broad ones.

Waiting. Most videos are judged quickly. A piece sitting flat after a day is telling you something, and the useful response is to make the next one differently rather than to hope.

Views that pay

Here is the part most creators miss. Views are worth money through more than one route, and the one that does not wait for a follower count is paid campaign briefs.

Picsart Earn publishes briefs and calculates payouts from real audience engagement, named on the program page as views, comments, shares, and reach on content you create and post to your own accounts. There is no follower minimum and no invite list. So the same work that gets a video seen is the work that decides what it earns.

That changes the maths on a good video. A piece that reaches a large audience earns from the brief it was made for, regardless of whether your account has cleared anyone else’s threshold. Briefs on the Earn campaigns board publish their reward logic before you start, so you know which actions count before you spend a day filming.

It also means the diagnostic work above is not just growth advice. Cutting two seconds off the front of a campaign video is, quite literally, a way to get paid more for the same idea.

Make the next one easier

Producing variations is what turns one decent idea into a format, and that is cheaper than it used to be.

Generate what you cannot film with the AI Video Generator, keep a recurring character consistent with Persona, and cut, caption and size everything in the Picsart Video Editor. The editing is where most of the difference between a video that holds and one that does not actually gets made.

Tips that move views on a small account

Start where the action already is

Cut the setup and open on the moment something is happening. Almost every underperforming video is slow to start, and the first second is the one that decides whether the rest gets watched at all.

Be specific with hashtags

TikTok names hashtags among the things it reads about a video, so tags that describe the actual subject tell it more than a pile of broad ones. Piling on generic tags does not widen reach on its own.

Reply to a comment with a video

A video reply becomes its own post and arrives with a question already attached, which is a reason for people to watch and answer. It also turns one piece that worked into a second one without a new idea.

Watch rewatches, not just views

A short loop watched three times by the same person counts three times. If a piece gets replayed, make more like it, because rewatchable content travels further than its runtime suggests.

Change one thing between attempts

Post a variation rather than a new idea: a different opening, a different sound, a different length. Changing everything at once tells you nothing about what actually helped.

Start with the video that flopped

Take a recent piece that underperformed, find the second where people left, and rebuild from there rather than starting something new. That one habit improves more videos than any posting schedule.

Then put the next one somewhere the result is measured. The Earn campaigns board pays on what the audience actually did, which is a faster way to find out whether a change worked than watching your own follower count.
